title: The Carpenter and the Poem-Lord
markdown:
The moon hung like a pearl against velvet. Under it, many seasons ago, Jun Mori worked in a workshop that smelled of sawdust and linseed oil. His hands were rough as bark and gentle as moss. He was known throughout the province for work that could weather a hundred storms and still stand, joints singing a silent song of resilience.

The lord of the grandest castle in the valley was Lord Hidetaka. His mind was a garden of verses. A perfect seventeen syllables, he often declared, could capture a bird’s song or the dewdrop on a spider’s thread. He arranged pebbles not for colour but for the stillness they evoked. When it came to his castle, that love of poetic perfection made him a peculiar master. He valued a sweeping eave that mimicked a heron’s wing more than the support it needed. The wind whispered through those eaves with a soft knowing sigh. Even the squirrels sometimes paused, as if listening for a hidden stanza.

One crisp autumn morning, the air smelling of fallen leaves and distant woodsmoke, Lord Hidetaka summoned Mori-san.

“Mori-san, my dear fellow of timber and truth,” he began, voice as light as a falling petal, thin mustache twitching, “I require a new wing. A wing that speaks of solitude, like a single crane in winter snow. A space that breathes with the quietude of a forgotten shrine.”

Mori-san bowed, eyes kind and weathered like old oak. “And what dimensions shall this wing possess? What manner of supports will please its solitary spirit?”

Lord Hidetaka waved a dismissive hand. “Dimensions are for builders of mundane bridges. This wing must be as the echo of a lonely flute. Imagine a roof that floats like a cloud, held aloft by the very essence of longing. The pillars must be so slender they are mere suggestions, like the memory of bamboo. They must whisper, not shout.” He plucked a fallen maple leaf from his sleeve and held it aloft. “This is the spirit I seek — ephemeral, yet profound.”

Mori-san looked at the leaf, delicate and dry, then at the solid stone of the castle walls. “A roof, even one as graceful as a cloud, needs something substantial to hold it against the sky. A strong wind can be a boisterous guest. Even the most profound longing requires a solid footing.”

Lord Hidetaka chuckled, a sound like dry reeds. “You speak of the practical. This is architectural poetry. I want the feeling of open space, the quiet of the void.” He recited, voice gaining a reedy enthusiasm, “Empty space holds all, / Echo answers silent call, / Nature’s breath is free. See? The void is key.”

And so it went. Mori-san sketched designs on rice paper of his own, showing where strong timbers would hide beneath decorative panels, where deep foundations would anchor the structure against weather and time. He explained, with the patience of a river, how the weight of roof tiles needed to be distributed, how walls would need to withstand the pressure of the earth should it decide to shift. Lord Hidetaka rejected them with a sigh that seemed to carry unfulfilled poetic dreams. “Too solid. It feels grounded. I want it to lift off with the morning mist. The pillars must be like ink strokes on rice paper, so fine that the light itself passes through them.” He would then recite a haiku about a solitary pine on a windswept cliff, expecting Mori-san to translate that sentiment into wood and plaster — a translation that, to Mori-san’s mind, seemed akin to asking a squirrel to compose a symphony.

One day, as Mori-san explained the necessity of a sturdy crossbeam, Lord Hidetaka’s mustache drooped. “Your mind is like a well-worn tool — practical, yes, but lacking imagination. This crossbeam is a clumsy word in my poem of a building. That curve should be a sigh, not a structural necessity.”

Mori-san looked at the half-finished wall, then up at the darkening sky. The wind, which had been a soft murmur in the pines, was beginning to tug at the eaves. It carried the scent of rain, heavy and insistent, a scent that always made Mori-san’s bones ache with a familiar premonition.

“My lord,” he said softly, “even the void needs edges to define it. And the wind does not care for poetry when it blows with anger. A castle must first be a home. And a home must be safe.”

Then the sky, which had been a placid blue, turned the bruised colour of plums. The wind, no longer a whisper, began to howl. Rain lashed the walls like a thousand tiny hammers. Inside the hastily constructed new wing, Lord Hidetaka’s design began to groan. The whispering pillars swayed. A section of the cloud-like roof sagged. A cascade of water poured in, drenching the lord’s meticulously arranged calligraphy scrolls. Lord Hidetaka, face as pale as a moth’s wing, silk robes suddenly damp, stared.

“The ink strokes. They are breaking.” He clutched his chest. “My solitude. My empty space.”

Mori-san, without a word, had already taken up his tools. His movements were not frantic but purposeful, honed by years of answering the earth’s rumblings and the sky’s tempests. He worked with a furious but controlled energy, speaking to each piece of timber, coaxing it to hold. He hammered in bracing timbers, reinforcing the weak points, ignoring the decorative flourishes Lord Hidetaka had insisted upon — the delicate carvings of cranes and bamboo that were now a liability. He drove in support beams, not like ink strokes, but like strong honest arms holding back the deluge. His hammer blows were a steady rhythm against the storm’s chaos. Perhaps these beams can be the roots of my cloud, my lord.

As the worst of the storm passed, the new wing, scarred and far from ethereal, still stood. It was not a poem. It was a shelter. The whispering pillars were now braced by sturdy timbers. The cloud-like roof had a few noticeable dips, but it had not surrendered.

Lord Hidetaka, shivering but safe, robes splattered with mud, looked at the repairs. He saw the raw strength of the wood, the clever joinery that had held. He noticed how the added beams, though rougher than he had intended, created a pleasing, almost rugged pattern.

“Mori-san,” he whispered, voice stripped of flourish, “you have saved my castle. You have saved me.” He looked at his own hands, which had only ever written verses and arranged flowers, then at Mori-san’s, calloused and strong. “There is a poetry in strength, isn’t there. A language spoken not in syllables, but in steadfastness.”

Mori-san simply nodded. He began to tidy his tools. The scent of wet wood and fresh rain filled the air.

In the seasons that followed, Lord Hidetaka did not abandon his haiku. Indeed, he found a new depth in them, a greater appreciation for the strength that allowed such delicate beauty. When he commissioned new additions, he stood with Mori-san and listened as the carpenter explained the whispers of the wood and the strengths of the stone. Mori-san closed the workshop shutter against a later, smaller wind, and the latch clicked — a small, ordinary sound, as sure as a well-cut joint. Outside, the eaves no longer sighed quite so freely. Inside, the sawdust settled, pale as moonlight, on a floor that had learned to hold.
characters: Jun Mori (a castle carpenter), Lord Hidetaka (a haiku-loving lord)
